biography.plain_text: Baron Johan Otto Valdemar Raben-Levetzau was a Danish landowner and museum founder based at Aalholm on Lolland. He inherited the estate from his father, former foreign minister Frederik Raben-Levetzau, and modernised its farming operations. His collection of historic cars became Aalholm Automobilmuseum, adding a public attraction to the family’s agricultural holdings.

long_biography.plain_text:
Baron Johan Otto Raben-Levetzau built his car collection around a 1911 Rolls-Royce that had survived on his family’s estate. He travelled abroad to find early vehicles and employed local craftsmen to restore them. Among his acquisitions was a Bugatti Type 57C with an altered bonnet, which he returned to its original configuration.

At Aalholm Automobilmuseum, the cars were displayed in four exhibition halls. Visitors could also ride a narrow-gauge steam railway through the park to the Baltic shore. He and his wife Elizabeth later opened rooms in the castle to the public, while continuing to live in a private wing.

Input age 87 is consistent with death age in 1992, not a living age in 2020. Calculated age fields are not edited. Exact unusual name and Danish context resolve the subject independently of the operator's mistaken Count title.

Father Frederik, brother Siegfried and son John are distinct people. The elder brother's successor-fund benefit is not assigned to this owner. Modern estate companies and social accounts belong to subsequent owners.

Original and terminal Agriculture concern productive inherited farmland and woodland, not the residence, noble title, personal boats or the car hobby. Retained core ownership is positively documented through death. Historical acreage is not represented as an unchanged terminal total.
Estate borrowing and asset disposals limit any estimate of personal net wealth. Later car auctions and foundation-owned museum property cannot be counted as his estate. No net-worth proposal is made.

Inherited is explicit for Aalholm; earlier lifetime transfers of associated estates do not erase that principal mechanism. Inherited-and-expanded is withheld: adding tourism and a collection does not establish material growth of the principal fortune.

Terminal relationship remains Unknown58 after testing Heir/family shareholder, Operator, Founder and passive owner. Son's co-ownership and historic tenancy do not prove who principally ran the core at death. Retrospective farming achievements do not establish a terminal operating mandate; no retirement inference from age.

Forbes-first and all supported link types searched: LinkedIn, Instagram, Personal Website, Facebook, Twitter/X, Youtube, TikTok, Wikipedia, Forbes, Vimeo, Flickr, Trip Advisor, Zillow and Company Website. No verified personal account or individual Wikipedia page found. Ancestor and father pages rejected. Current castle website is subsequent ownership, so no company link proposed.

One historical family compilation reports 1903, conflicting with the convergent 1904 biography/genealogy and age 87 at February 1992 death. The corroborated 1904 date is proposed at bounded confidence. Source differences on initial Beldringe transfer and posthumous estate sale years are omitted from biography.

Contemporary guide sections were fully available in indexed text even though the PDF has no extraction layer. Local obituary and environmental history were read directly as complete relevant PDF pages. Present estate essays are retrospective, not treated as primary contemporary proof.

The minimum two tags separate notable collecting practice and museum-founding status. No unsupported aristocracy, agricultural literal tag, Automotive wealth sector or gambling activity is inferred. Vessel promotional stories do not establish a material casino business.
Published prose omits political and family-dispute material outside this requested business/biographical scope; the research does not deny or adjudicate it.
